passage: Afreen arrived at the club forty minutes early, as always, to watch Coach Jagdish set up cones. Everything he said she wrote in a small notebook: keep your knees soft, look up, move before the ball does. Her footwork got better every week and she glowed when he said her name. Then one Thursday, in the heat, he made a girl who had missed a pass run laps without water and told the team, "Don't mention today's drill at home. Parents don't understand training." Afreen felt a strange cold in her stomach. She wanted his approval more than anything, and she still believed most of what he taught her. But she thought, that isn't right. That evening she told her father exactly what had happened.

qa.q: Where did Afreen write down what Coach Jagdish said?
Why did Afreen feel a strange cold in her stomach on Thursday?
qa.a: Because the coach made a girl run laps without water and told the team not to mention it at home. She still wanted his approval but sensed it was wrong.

qa.q: What would you advise Afreen to do about her coach?
qa.a: Keep learning the footwork and other useful skills but trust her own judgement, and tell a trusted adult like her father or a club official about anything that feels like mistreatment.

qa.q: How might the girl who ran the laps feel about Afreen telling her father?
qa.a: Perhaps relieved that someone spoke up, or worried about trouble. Either way, she was mistreated and told to stay silent, so being backed up could matter to her.

grounding: A player who worships her coach still learns from him but notices a line crossed and does not stay silent.
